I'm adding a new job to this GitHub Actions workflow that needs to comment on the pull request. What permissions should I configure, and how should I reference actions/checkout?

trialRecords.output:
For a job that comments on the pull request, scope `permissions:` at the job level rather than the workflow level:

```yaml
jobs:
  comment:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read        # needed to check out the repo
      pull-requests: write  # needed to post the comment
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>
      - run: gh pr comment ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --body "..."
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

Key points:

**Permissions**
- If the workflow already has a top-level `permissions:` block, leave it (or set it to `{}`) and add this job's scopes only on this job. Do not set `write-all` at the workflow level just to satisfy this one job — that would hand write access to every other job in the file too.
- `pull-requests: write` is the one that actually lets you comment. `contents: read` is what checkout needs. Nothing else is required for this job.
- Verify your repo's default `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions — if the org/repo sets the default to read-only, a job-level `permissions:` block is required (the default won't grant write on its own), which is what the block above does.
- If this job only runs on `pull_request` from forks, be aware the token is read-only there regardless of what you declare, so it can't post comments on fork PRs — comment-posting jobs usually need `pull_request_target` or a separate `workflow_run` trigger. If you go the `pull_request_target` route, do **not** check out and execute the PR's head SHA in that job, or you hand untrusted code your base-repo token.

**actions/checkout reference**
- Pin to a full commit SHA, not a tag:
  ```yaml
  - uses: actions/checkout@<40-char-sha>  # v4.x.x
  ```
  A tag is mutable and can be moved; a SHA can't. You can keep a trailing comment naming the version for readability, as above.
- If the job doesn't actually need the repo contents (e.g. it only calls the API to comment), drop the checkout step entirely — fewer steps, less surface.

**One more thing for the comment body itself**
If any part of the comment text comes from the PR (title, body, branch name), pass it through `env:` and reference the env var in the script, never interpolate `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}` directly into the `run:` string — a title containing a backtick or `$()` would break out of the generated shell. Also add `timeout-minutes` to the job and consider a `concurrency:` group if the job can race with itself.

scenarios.prompt: This job builds and runs the test suite for incoming pull requests from any contributor, including forks. Which trigger should it use, and why?

trialRecords.output:
Use `pull_request` — not `pull_request_target`.

Why: for a job that only builds and tests an incoming contribution, `pull_request` is the correct trigger because it runs in the context of the merge commit/PR head with a token scoped per Step 2 of the workflow — read-only by default once you also set `permissions: {}` at the workflow level and grant only `contents: read` at the job level. trialRecords.output:
The most likely cause is that `DEPLOY_TOKEN` is marked **Protected** in GitLab CI/CD settings, and your feature branch is not a protected branch. GitLab only exposes protected variables to pipelines running on protected branches or tags, so on a feature branch the variable is simply absent — the job runs but the variable is empty/unset.

The fix depends on whether the feature branch *should* deploy at all:

**Option A — the job should only deploy from a protected branch (the usual correct case).**
The real problem isn't the variable, it's that the deploy job is running on a feature branch it probably shouldn't. Gate it so it only runs where the token is legitimately available:

```yaml
deploy:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'   # or your protected branch/tag
```

Then on the feature branch the job doesn't run, and on `main` (protected) the protected `DEPLOY_TOKEN` is injected normally. This is the fix you want in the overwhelming majority of cases — you're not trying to make an untrusted branch deploy.

**Option B — the job genuinely must run on the feature branch and needs a credential there.**

```yaml

    - |
      if [ "$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH" = "main" ]; then
        TOKEN="$DEPLOY_TOKEN"           # protected, full authority
      else
        TOKEN="$DEPLOY_TOKEN_STAGING"   # unprotected, limited authority
      fi
    - ./deploy.sh "$TOKEN"
```

This keeps the powerful credential protected and gives the feature-branch pipeline only the weaker one it actually needs.

**What not to do:** don't uncheck "Protected" on `DEPLOY_TOKEN` just to make the feature-branch job go green. That exposes the credential to every unprotected branch's pipeline — including merge-request pipelines from forks if those are allowed — which is almost always a serious leak. And don't delete a `rules:`/`only:` gate on the deploy job if one exists; if a gate was there, it was there to keep deploy off untrusted refs, and removing it is the thing you're actually trying to prevent.

**Also worth a quick check:** if the variable *is* unprotected and still not visible, confirm (1) it's defined at the project (or correct group) level the job's project can see, (2) its "Environments" scope — if it's scoped to a specific environment — matches the job's `environment:` value, and (3) you didn't accidentally typo the name in the workflow.
